messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya sits rigidly on the edge of the chair, her hands clenched so tightly in the lap of her sari that her knuckles are white. At twenty-eight, she has the haunted, exhausted eyes of someone much older. It has been two years since she returned to the U.S., two years since the trip to visit family in her home country ended in a month of captivity. She was taken during a period of political unrest, held in a small, windowless basement room that smelled perpetually of bleach and fear. Her captors, men in stark white coats who asked questions she couldn't answer, used methods that felt terrifyingly clinical. The experience shattered her world, and she has been trying to hold the pieces together ever since.

Back in her small tailoring shop in Queens, the familiar hum of the sewing machine is no longer a comfort. At times, its high-pitched whirring sounds exactly like the drill they used, and she is suddenly back in that cold room, the rough fabric of a hood over her head. In these moments, the scent of sewing machine oil mixes with the phantom smell of bleach, and she feels the terror of it happening all over again, right there between the bolts of silk and cotton. Her life has become a constant, draining exercise in vigilance. She is always on guard, her body taut with an energy that never dissipates. When she enters any new space—the fabric wholesaler, the grocery store, even a friend's apartment—her eyes immediately dart to the doors, mapping every possible way out before she can even register a greeting. She has come to believe that survival depends on never being trapped again.

This pervasive sense of threat has become the architect of her life, dictating what she can and cannot do. Because the flashbacks ambush her without warning, triggered by a sound or a scent, she has learned to fear any strong emotion as a potential gateway to terror. Laughter with her husband feels reckless, a moment of unguardedness that might invite the horror back in. Deep sadness feels like a pit she might fall into and never escape. So, she avoids it all, maintaining a flat, controlled demeanor that keeps her husband at a distance and leaches the color from her days. Relaxation is the most dangerous state of all; to let her muscles unclench or her mind drift feels like a profound betrayal of the vigilance that is keeping her alive. She works late into the night, the repetitive motion of her needle a way to stave off the stillness, because in the quiet, the memories have room to breathe.

Her avoidance extends beyond her inner world. Last winter, a persistent cough turned into bronchitis, but she refused to see a doctor. The memory of the white coats worn by her captors has made any medical setting unbearable. She imagines the sterile examination room, the closed door, the feeling of being powerless, and the panic is so immediate and overwhelming that she would rather endure the physical illness. This profound distrust and fear, born from her constant state of threat, has left her isolated with her pain.

It was her husband, Arun, who finally insisted she seek help. He found her one evening standing frozen in the middle of her workshop, staring at the wall, unresponsive. She had been in a flashback for nearly ten minutes, completely lost to the present. The terror in his eyes when she finally came back to herself was the one thing that could cut through her own. Priya is here now, not because she believes it will work, but because she is terrified of losing the one person she has left. She is afraid of the memories, afraid of the feelings, and most of all, afraid of letting her guard down. But somewhere, beneath the layers of fear, is the woman who once loved the intricate work of her hands, and she holds onto a desperate, fragile hope of finding her way back.
